newsitem.title: USA: TWA opens labor talks with pilots union.
newsitem.headline: TWA opens labor talks with pilots union.

text.p: Trans World Airlines Inc. and its pilots union began labour talks Wednesday that are expected to continue for at least one year and may result in only minimal wage increases for the pilots, industry experts said.
TWA, the nation's seventh largest carrier, said contract negotations started Wednesay but declined to comment on the opening proposals.

"We are hoping and expecting that we will have a productive series of negotiations. We have a good working relationship with the pilots and we don't expect anything but a win-win situation for everyone involved," said Donn Walker, a spokesman for the airline.
The pilots union did not return calls seeking comment.

While pilots at other carriers such as AMR Corp.'s American Airlines and UAL Corp.'s United Airlines recently secured sizable pay increases, the prospects for TWA's pilots are different, analysts said.
TWA is struggling with a dwindling cash supply, recent management turnover, an ageing fleet and the aftermath of last year's crash of Flight 800, analysts said.
TWA's pilots have already made concessions to help the St. Louis-based carrier through two bankruptcy reorganizations, analysts said.
"There is no room for the pilots to make more concessions. They are already paid about a third less than the rest of the industry," said Stephen Klein, an airline analyst with S&P Equity Group.
"If talks drag on for a while, TWA may have a (financial) turnaround. If they don't, they may forced to give up more equity to their employees," Klein said.
TWA's employees currently own about 30 percent of the company.

The Air Line Pilots Association previously said it is seeking "substantial improvements in scheduling and pay rates comparable to (its) counterparts at other major airlines." The union said its pilots now make about 40 percent less than pilots at rival airlines.
When the union asked the airline to begin contract negotiations, the pilots said they understood that the compay has suffered recent financial losses.
But the union contended that other airlines have been able to "operate profitably with higher pilot pay rates and more efficient scheduling."

TWA recently posted a first quarter loss of $71.6 million, or $1.54 a share, on revenue of $762.3 million. The results were better than Wall Street expectations but the losses exceeded the airline's 1996 first quarter loss of $37.1 million, or $1.46 a share, on revenues of $782.4 million.
Analysts said TWA must focus on shoring up its balance sheet before it can offer better wages for the employees.
"First things first. Profits first. Pay raises second," said Samuel Buttrick, an airline analyst with PaineWebber.
TWA faces a full range of labour negotiations this year, since contracts for the pilots, machinists and flight attendants all become amendable later this year.
The pilot's current contract, which began Sept. 1, 1994, becomes amendable on August 30.
TWA is just one of several airlines facing labour talks with its pilots this year.

American Airlines had a contentious series of negotiations that included a brief strike and intervention by President Clinton. US Airways Group Inc. and Continental Airlines Inc. are also in the midst of contract talks with its pilots.
